questions.problem:
Which of the following are elementary matrices?

$$
W=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ \frac{3}{4} & 1\end{aligned}],\,Y=[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{4} & 0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}],\,Z=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -4 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$
questions.worked_solution:
An elementary matrix is a matrix obtained from the identity matrix by applying exactly one elementary row operation. 

With that in mind, let's examine our matrices.

- The matrix $W$ is an elementary matrix because it can be obtained from ${I}_{2}$ by applying the elementary row operation ${R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+\frac{3}{4}{R}_{1},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+\frac{3}{4}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ \frac{3}{4} & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =W\end{aligned}
$$

- The matrix $Y$ is not an elementary matrix because it can't be obtained from ${I}_{2}$ by applying only one elementary row operation.

- The matrix $Z$ is an elementary matrix because it can be obtained from ${I}_{2}$ by applying the elementary row operation ${R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-4){R}_{1},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-4){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -4 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =Z\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, only $W$ and $Z$ are elementary matrices.

questions.problem:
Which of the following are elementary matrices?

$$
Q=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}],\,W=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 7\end{aligned}],\,E=[\begin{aligned}1 & -4 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$
questions.worked_solution:
An elementary matrix is a matrix obtained from the identity matrix by applying exactly one elementary row operation. 

With that in mind, let's examine our matrices.

- The matrix $Q$ is an elementary matrix because it can be obtained from ${I}_{2}$ by applying the elementary row operation ${R}_{2}:=3{R}_{2},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & {R}_{2}:=3{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =Q\end{aligned}
$$

- The matrix $W$ is not an elementary matrix because it can't be obtained from ${I}_{2}$ by applying only one elementary row operation.

- The matrix $E$ is an elementary matrix because it can be obtained from ${I}_{2}$ by applying the elementary row operation ${R}_{1}:={R}_{1}+(-4){R}_{2},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & {R}_{1}:={R}_{1}+(-4){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -4 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =E\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, only $Q$ and $E$ are elementary matrices.

$$
questions.worked_solution:
An elementary matrix is a matrix obtained from the identity matrix by applying exactly one elementary row operation. 

With that in mind, let's examine our matrices.

- The matrices $A$ and $C$ are not elementary matrices because they can't be obtained from ${I}_{2}$ by applying only one elementary row operation.

$$

questions.problem:
Which of the following are elementary matrices?

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}],\,B=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}],\,C=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 4 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$
questions.worked_solution:
An elementary matrix is a matrix obtained from the identity matrix by applying exactly one elementary row operation. 

With that in mind, let's examine our matrices.

- The matrix $A$ is an elementary matrix because it can be obtained from ${I}_{2}$ by applying the elementary row operation ${R}_{2}:={R}_{1}+{R}_{2},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & {R}_{1}:={R}_{1}+{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =A\end{aligned}
$$

- The matrix $B$ is an elementary matrix because it can be obtained from ${I}_{2}$ by applying the elementary row operation ${R}_{1}↔{R}_{2},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & {R}_{1}↔{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =B\end{aligned}
$$

- The matrix $C$ is not an elementary matrix because it can't be obtained from ${I}_{2}$ by applying only one elementary row operation.

Therefore, only $A$ and $B$ are elementary matrices.

questions.problem:
Find the inverse of the elementary matrix 
$K=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 8 & 1\end{aligned}].$
questions.worked_solution:
We write down $K$ and the identity matrix $I$ side-by-side (as shown below) and apply an elementary row operation that transforms the left matrix into the identity matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}[K\,|\,I\,] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 8 & 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-8){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -8 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The inverse is obtained on the right-hand side of our big matrix after the transformation. Therefore, 

$$
{K}^{-1}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -8 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

questions.worked_solution:
Notice that ${E}_{1}$ and ${E}_{2}$ are both elementary matrices.

First, we need to find ${E}_{2}^{-1}.$ We write down ${E}_{2}$ and the identity matrix $I$ side-by-side (as shown below) and apply an elementary row operation that transforms the left matrix into the identity matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}[{E}_{2}\,|\,I\,] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -\frac{1}{2} & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & {R}_{2}:=(-2){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & -2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{2}^{-1} & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can find the product ${E}_{1}{E}_{2}^{-1}:$

$$
{E}_{1}{E}_{2}^{-1}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -2 & -2\end{aligned}]
$$
